Purple sandpipers Calidris maritima breeding in the high Arctic exhibit a life history characterized by a single annual reproductive event. Females typically produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a pattern that reflects the extreme brevity of the tundra growing season and the energetic demands of egg production. Under the warm-body thermal conditions typical of an actively incubating adult, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time elapsed since birth at which these birds achieve their first brood is approximately 1095 days [tR = approximately 1095 days], a considerable delay that underscores the protracted maturation period required for this long-lived shorebird to accumulate sufficient body condition for successful nesting. This relatively late onset of reproduction is consistent with the slow pace of life observed among high-latitude scolopacids.

Eggs deposited in tundra scrapes are incubated primarily by the male at a mean nest temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a thermal regime that governs the rate of embryonic development. Under these conditions, the age at birth, measured as the interval between oviposition and hatching, is 22 days [ab = 22 days] at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This incubation period is modest in length compared to larger arctic-breeding waders, but it is tightly constrained by the short snow-free season. Newly hatched chicks emerge weighing 9.1 grams [Wwb = 9.1 grams], a relatively high birth mass for a calidridine sandpiper, likely an adaptation that reduces the vulnerability of precocial young to thermal stress and predation on the open tundra. The downy chicks are capable of leaving the nest within hours of hatching, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth that is sustained by intensive parental brooding and foraging on abundant insect larvae. This growth phase relies heavily on the abundant arthropod supply emerging from the tundra in the brief polar summer. Chicks must double their mass rapidly to meet the energetic demands of thermoregulation and locomotion, a challenge compounded by the low ambient temperatures that persist even during the summer solstice in the high Arctic.

The transition to independent flight marks a critical developmental milestone in the annual cycle of the Purple sandpiper. Under the metabolically active body temperature of approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 22 days [tx = 22 days], a remarkably brief nestling period for a shorebird of this body size. This accelerated developmental trajectory is ecologically necessary: fledglings must achieve flight capability before the onset of cold weather and the southward migration that begins in late summer. The precocial mode of development means that young birds attain flight feathers quickly, with the post-hatching period dominated by feather growth and the refinement of foraging skills on intertidal habitats rather than by prolonged dependency on parental provisioning. This rapid achievement of fledging allows juveniles to accumulate the fat reserves necessary for their first long-distance migration to wintering grounds along rocky coastlines.

Gonadal maturation follows a slower schedule than skeletal development. The time since birth at puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive cycling, is 66 days [tp = 66 days] when measured at the typical active body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This timing indicates that while fledglings are fully mobile and self-sufficient within weeks of hatching, sexual maturation is deferred well beyond the first summer, a pattern that is widespread among long-lived scolopacids that delay reproduction until they have acquired adult plumage and sufficient body reserves. The interval between fledging and puberty represents a period of continued physiological investment in skeletal ossification, feather replacement, and the development of foraging efficiency on the exposed rocky shores they inhabit. Juvenile birds thus spend their first year in a non-reproductive state, focusing instead on building the nutritional capital needed for future breeding.

Adult body mass shows considerable variation across the annual cycle, with birds reaching an ultimate wet weight of 90 grams [Wwi = 90 grams] during the pre-migratory fattening period. Field records indicate that the ultimate wet weight ranges from 50 to 105 grams (50-105 grams) [Wwi = 50-105 grams], a wide span reflecting seasonal changes in body condition, with lean birds in midwinter and hyperphagic individuals in late autumn storing extensive lipid reserves. Under the thermal conditions of an actively foraging bird at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum lifespan has been estimated at approximately 7592 days [am = approximately 7592 days], a value equivalent to roughly 20.8 years, making the Purple sandpiper one of the longer-lived members of the genus Calidris. This extreme longevity, combined with the low annual fecundity of one clutch per year, places the species firmly in the slow end of the life-history continuum among Arctic-breeding shorebirds, a strategy viable only in stable, low-predation environments.
